VIDEO.title: The Most FRIGHTENING Verse in the Bible... (Matthew 7:13-29)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Hear these words, and do them.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 7:13-29: the narrow gate, false prophets in sheep's clothing, trees known by their fruit, 'Lord, Lord,' and the wise and foolish builders. The crowds are astonished at His authority.

The audience is the same as for chapters 5-7: Jesus, His disciples, and crowds from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan (4:25). As the sermon ends it retreads its earlier themes, which the video reads as a chiasm.

'The Law and the Prophets' (5:17; 7:12) is shorthand for the whole Tanakh. The video argues that 'fulfill' and 'abolish' are idioms for interpreting Scripture well or badly, so the sermon is Jesus' true interpretation of God's word, bookended by that phrase.

Like a first-century rabbi, Jesus drops hints (remez) from the Old Testament: the gate of Lady Wisdom and the house of Lady Folly (Proverbs 8-9), the evening wolves (Zephaniah 3:3), the fruitful tree (Psalm 1), and Wisdom's house (Proverbs 9:1).
Halakha, 'the walk,' is how one lives out the Torah; the deeds are its fruit. A person's actions prove their theology, as James 2 argues. The false prophets look religious but bear rotten fruit.

Who are they? Jeremiah 23:11 says prophet and priest are polluted. The video says Jesus means the religious leaders: priests, scribes, Sadducees and corrupt Pharisees. It is possible to know and teach God's word and be far from Him. Watch the fruit, measured by the Beatitudes.
QUOTES: Like any good Jewish rabbi in the first century, Jesus is not pulling these images out of thin air. He's pulling them from the Old Testament.
The actions of a person proves their theology.
They may look like the same gate for those who don't know any better, but they're not.
It's very possible to be in love with your ministry for God more than the actual God of your ministry.
The evidence is more obvious than you think it is.

method.p: The teacher's tip: when Jesus mentions a gate, a wolf, a tree or a house, stop and ask where Israel's Scriptures used that picture. Find the passage, read it whole, and bring it back to the sermon. Rewatch the video and chew on it.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it.
Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father who is in heaven will enter.
Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and does them, may be compared to a wise man who built his house on the rock.

left.text: Beside the gates, at the opening to the city, / At the entrance of the doors, she makes a shout:

right.text: But he does not know that the dead are there, / That those she called are in the depths of Sheol.

lines.text: Gates are where Wisdom takes her stand. But Lady Folly also calls to those who pass by, from the doorway of her house, offering what looks like the same thing; her path leads to death.
'Enter through the narrow gate' takes the disciples back to the choice between wisdom and foolishness. The gates may look alike; the difference is obedience to Jesus' words (7:24, 26).

Chrysostom: 'look not to this, says He, that it is rough and narrow, but where it ends; nor that the opposite is wide and spacious, but where it issues' (Homilies on Matthew 23). Compare 'I set before you the way of life and the way of death' (Jeremiah 21:8).

src.text: Her princes in her midst are roaring lions; / Her judges are wolves at evening; / They leave nothing to gnaw for the morning. / Her prophets are reckless, treacherous men; / Her priests have profaned the sanctuary. / They have done violence to the law.

lines.text: In Zephaniah God calls Jerusalem's officials evening wolves, when wolves are hungriest. The very ones meant to judge and prophesy God's word do violence to His law.
Some of the most corrupt leaders will take Jesus' life and persecute His disciples. The warning is not theoretical.
Ezekiel uses the same picture: 'Her princes within her are like wolves tearing the prey' (Ezekiel 22:27). Paul warns the Ephesian elders of 'savage wolves' (Acts 20:29).

src.text: How blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, / Nor stand in the way of sinners, / Nor sit in the seat of scoffers! / But his delight is in the law of Yahweh, / And in His law he meditates day and night. / And he will be like a tree firmly planted by streams of water, / Which yields its fruit in its season

lines.text: 'Every good tree bears good fruit' (7:17): you are meant to think of Psalm 1. Jesus calls His disciples to choose the way of true wisdom over the false teachers.
John the Baptist used the picture first: 'every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire' (3:10), the same words as 7:19.

left.text: Wisdom has built her house, / She has hewn out her seven pillars;

right.text: Forsake your simplicity and live, / And step into the way of understanding.

lines.text: Wisdom builds her house and sets a banquet for all who will listen. Jesus ends His sermon with the same call: hear and do, and build on the rock.
Luke adds that the wise man 'dug and went deep, and laid a foundation on the rock' (Luke 6:48). In Galilee, dry wadis can become torrents after winter rain.

left.text: Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.

right.text: Therefore, in all things, whatever you want people to do for you, so do for them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.

lines.text: The phrase is shorthand for the whole Tanakh: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings), the Christian Old Testament. Jesus bookends the sermon with it to show that the sermon is about rightly interpreting and living out God's word.
Matthew 5:21-7:12 is the body of the sermon. In the kingdom of God, God's people obey Him, and in obeying they spread His kingdom.

left.text: For I say to you that unless your righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

right.text: Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father who is in heaven will enter.

lines.text: The fruit Jesus wants far exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees. Both groups give, pray and fast; the difference is the heart.

left.text: Let your light shine before men in such a way that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

right.text: Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and does them, may be compared to a wise man who built his house on the rock.

lines.text: Building on the rock retreads being a light to the world: radical fruit that everyone will see, giving glory to the Father.

src.text: For both prophet and priest are polluted; / Even in My house I have found their evil,” declares Yahweh.

lines.text: The word does not mean pagan; these men were highly religious. The video: Jesus means the religious leaders of God's people: the priests, the scribes, the Sadducees, the corrupt Pharisees.
Jeremiah goes on: 'They speak a vision of their own heart, / Not from the mouth of Yahweh' (Jeremiah 23:16).

src.text: If a brother or sister is without clothing and in need of daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and be filled,” and yet you do not give them what is necessary for their body, what use is that?

lines.text: Halakha (from the Hebrew for 'walk') is how a person walks out the Torah; the video calls the deeds the fruit on the tree of halakha. If a teacher's theology does not make him lowly, merciful, loving and radically generous, the fruit is rotten, whatever he teaches.
James makes the same argument, with an outcast who cannot clothe or feed himself.

src.text: Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, in Your name did we not prophesy, and in Your name cast out demons, and in Your name do many miracles?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness.’

lines.text: It is possible for respected religious leaders who teach and observe God's word with authority to be far from the Lord and ignore what matters to Him.
Chrysostom calls it 'that fearful saying, I never knew you' (Homilies on Matthew 24). Jesus says later, 'Many false prophets will arise and will deceive many' (24:11).

PEOPLE.name: Jesus

PEOPLE.video: The same audience for all three chapters, from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan.
PEOPLE.bg: The crowds 'were astonished at His teaching' (7:28).

PEOPLE.name: The false prophets
PEOPLE.video: Look religious, say the right things, but their fruit is rotten. The video names the priests, scribes, Sadducees and corrupt Pharisees.
PEOPLE.bg: Matthew's Gospel will show the conflict with these leaders growing (chapters 9, 12, 23).

PEOPLE.name: Lady Wisdom and Lady Folly
PEOPLE.video: The two women of Proverbs 8-9 who both call from the gates and heights; only one leads to life.
PEOPLE.bg: Proverbs 1-9 is framed as a father's teaching to his son about choosing wisdom.

PEOPLE.name: Zephaniah and Jeremiah
PEOPLE.video: Prophets whose rebukes of Jerusalem's officials, prophets and priests Jesus echoes.
PEOPLE.bg: Both preached in Judah in the late 600s BC, before the Babylonian exile.

PEOPLE.name: James
PEOPLE.video: Quoted for 'faith without works': actions prove theology.
PEOPLE.bg: James the brother of the Lord, traditionally the author of the letter.

TERMS.def: The Hebrew Bible: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets), Ketuvim (Writings). 'The Law and the Prophets' points to it.
A 'hint': a short phrase that calls a whole Old Testament passage to mind. The captions spell it several ways.
From the Hebrew for 'walk': how one lives out the Torah day to day.
Commandments (singular mitzvah), and by extension the good deeds that obey them. The video calls them the fruit on the tree of halakha.
A mirrored pattern; the video reads the sermon's ending as echoing its beginning.
Those who claim to speak for God but do not (Jeremiah 23:16). Jesus says they are known by their fruits.
Literally 'without law': the charge against those who never obeyed (7:23).
The right and power to command. Jesus taught on His own authority (7:29).

WORDS.gloss: Gate: a city or temple gate.
To press hard; 'constricted' (LSB). Related to thlipsis, tribulation.
Godless, profane (the related adjective; 'hypocrite' in older English Bibles).

BACKGROUND.p: The gate was where elders judged, business was done and news was shared. In Proverbs, Wisdom stands at the gates to call the city.
Wolves were a real danger to flocks. Prophets used them for rulers who preyed on the people (Zephaniah 3:3; Ezekiel 22:27).
Houses were built of basalt stones. In the rainy season, dry stream beds can flood suddenly; a house on bedrock stands, one on sand washes out.
Scribes taught by citing earlier teachers. Jesus' 'But I say to you' in chapter 5 stunned the crowds (7:28-29).

WITNESSES.text: But look not to this, says He, that it is rough and narrow, but where it ends; nor that the opposite is wide and spacious, but where it issues.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 23, on 7:13-14. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: He calls the steadfastness of His doctrine a rock; because in truth His commands are stronger than any rock, setting one above all the waves of human affairs.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 24, on 7:24-25. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: But they were astonished most of all at His authority.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 25, on 7:28-29. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: The video holds this view, popular in some Jewish-roots teaching. Many scholars read 'fulfill' in Matthew as bringing to its intended goal, as with prophecy fulfilled (1:22; 2:15). Either way, 5:17-48 shows Jesus giving the true sense of the Law.
The video: the Jewish religious leaders of Jesus' day. Others see a warning for the church's future too, as in 24:11 and Acts 20:29-30.
Several outlines propose a mirrored shape (for example the bookends 5:17 and 7:12). Not every scholar agrees on the details.

DEBATES.h: Does 7:21-23 deny that the miracles happened?
DEBATES.p: Jesus does not dispute their claims; He says He never knew them. Works done 'in Your name' are not the same as doing the Father's will.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: On screen the fruitful tree is Psalm 1:1-3 (the captions say 'Psalm 11 1:3'), and the evening wolves are Zephaniah 3:3 (the captions say 'Zephaniah 33').
Mitzvot literally means 'commandments' (singular mitzvah). It is also used for good deeds, which is the video's point.

In Jeremiah 23:11 the Hebrew is the verb chanaph (H2610), 'polluted' in the LSB. The 'hypocrite' sense belongs to the related word chaneph (H2611), 'godless' in the LSB (Job 8:13), which older English Bibles render 'hypocrite.'
That 'abolish' and 'fulfill' are idioms for interpreting is the video's view; scholars debate it (see Debates).
In the video's reading of 5:17, 'the Law of the Prophets' should be 'the Law or the Prophets.'

QUESTIONS: What makes the narrow gate hard to find, and the wide gate easy to walk through?
The video says the two gates can look alike. How would you tell Wisdom's call from Folly's today?
How would you check a teacher's fruit against the Beatitudes, without becoming the judge 7:1-5 warns about?
Is it possible to love your ministry for God more than God? What are the warning signs?
Which of Jesus' words in chapters 5-7 are you hearing but not yet doing?
Rewatch the video, as the teacher suggests. What did you notice the second time?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: it is possible for respected religious leaders who teach and observe God's word with authority to be far from the Lord and ignore what matters to Him. Disciples should watch not just what teachers say, however correct, but whether their fruit matches the sermon. For us: are there those who know and teach God's word but are far from the Lord in their hearts? You will know by watching what they do, and seeing if it aligns with the Beatitudes and Jesus' examples. Think about how this applies to your life so that you can do something about it.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): turn the test on yourself first (7:5). Pick one Beatitude this week and ask, 'Does my life bear this fruit?' Then do one concrete thing Jesus said in chapters 5-7, since the wise builder is the one who 'hears these words of Mine and does them' (7:24).

- Halakha, 'the walk,' is how one lives out the Torah; the deeds are its fruit. A person's actions prove their theology, as James 2 argues. The false prophets look religious but bear rotten fruit.
- Who are they? Jeremiah 23:11 says prophet and priest are polluted. The video says Jesus means the religious leaders: priests, scribes, Sadducees and corrupt Pharisees. It is possible to know and teach God's word and be far from Him. Watch the fruit, measured by the Beatitudes.

   Wisdom's invitation (Proverbs 9:6, LSB): "Forsake your simplicity and live, / And step into the way of understanding."
   (video) Wisdom builds her house and sets a banquet for all who will listen. Jesus ends His sermon with the same call: hear and do, and build on the rock.
   [Background] Luke adds that the wise man 'dug and went deep, and laid a foundation on the rock' (Luke 6:48). In Galilee, dry wadis can become torrents after winter rain. (Luke 6:46-49)

## The sermon's bookends
1. Bookend · 5:17 and 7:12: The Law and the Prophets
   Start (Matthew 5:17, LSB): "Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill."
   End (Matthew 7:12, LSB): "Therefore, in all things, whatever you want people to do for you, so do for them, for this is the Law and the Prophets."
   (video) The phrase is shorthand for the whole Tanakh: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings), the Christian Old Testament. Jesus bookends the sermon with it to show that the sermon is about rightly interpreting and living out God's word.
   [Background] Matthew 5:21-7:12 is the body of the sermon. In the kingdom of God, God's people obey Him, and in obeying they spread His kingdom.
2. Echo · 5:20 and 7:21: A greater righteousness
   Start (Matthew 5:20, LSB): "For I say to you that unless your righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven."
   End (Matthew 7:21, LSB): "Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father who is in heaven will enter."
   (video) The fruit Jesus wants far exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees. Both groups give, pray and fast; the difference is the heart.
3. Echo · 5:16 and 7:24: Light that people can see
   Start (Matthew 5:16, LSB): "Let your light shine before men in such a way that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven."
   End (Matthew 7:24, LSB): "Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and does them, may be compared to a wise man who built his house on the rock."
   (video) Building on the rock retreads being a light to the world: radical fruit that everyone will see, giving glory to the Father.

## Known by their fruit
1. Who are they? · Jeremiah 23: Prophet and priest are polluted
   Leaders Jeremiah 23:11: "For both prophet and priest are polluted; / Even in My house I have found their evil,” declares Yahweh." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Jeremiah+23:11
   (video) The word does not mean pagan; these men were highly religious. The video: Jesus means the religious leaders of God's people: the priests, the scribes, the Sadducees, the corrupt Pharisees.
   [Background] Jeremiah goes on: 'They speak a vision of their own heart, / Not from the mouth of Yahweh' (Jeremiah 23:16). (Jeremiah 23:16)
2. The test · Matthew 7:16-20: Actions prove theology
   Fruit James 2:15-16: "If a brother or sister is without clothing and in need of daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and be filled,” and yet you do not give them what is necessary for their body, what use is that?" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=James+2:15-16
   (video) Halakha (from the Hebrew for 'walk') is how a person walks out the Torah; the video calls the deeds the fruit on the tree of halakha. If a teacher's theology does not make him lowly, merciful, loving and radically generous, the fruit is rotten, whatever he teaches.
   (video) James makes the same argument, with an outcast who cannot clothe or feed himself. (James 2:14-17)
3. The frightening verse · Matthew 7:21-23: I never knew you
   Warning Matthew 7:22-23: "Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, in Your name did we not prophesy, and in Your name cast out demons, and in Your name do many miracles?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness.’" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+7:22-23
   (video) It is possible for respected religious leaders who teach and observe God's word with authority to be far from the Lord and ignore what matters to Him.
   [Background] Chrysostom calls it 'that fearful saying, I never knew you' (Homilies on Matthew 24). Jesus says later, 'Many false prophets will arise and will deceive many' (24:11). (Matthew 24:11; Matthew 24:24)

## Key people
- Jesus: Ends the sermon with a choice: hear His words and do them, or not. He teaches with authority. [Background] 'Not as their scribes' (7:29): the scribes cited earlier teachers; Jesus says 'I say to you.'
- The disciples and the crowds: The same audience for all three chapters, from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan. [Background] The crowds 'were astonished at His teaching' (7:28).
- The false prophets: Look religious, say the right things, but their fruit is rotten. The video names the priests, scribes, Sadducees and corrupt Pharisees. [Background] Matthew's Gospel will show the conflict with these leaders growing (chapters 9, 12, 23).
- Lady Wisdom and Lady Folly: The two women of Proverbs 8-9 who both call from the gates and heights; only one leads to life. [Background] Proverbs 1-9 is framed as a father's teaching to his son about choosing wisdom.
- Zephaniah and Jeremiah: Prophets whose rebukes of Jerusalem's officials, prophets and priests Jesus echoes. [Background] Both preached in Judah in the late 600s BC, before the Babylonian exile.
- James: Quoted for 'faith without works': actions prove theology. [Background] James the brother of the Lord, traditionally the author of the letter.

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum (named in the video): Near the traditional site of the sermon by the lake.
- Jerusalem (named in the video): Seat of the priests and the temple: the 'officials of Jerusalem' in the video's reading.
- Hippos: A Decapolis city across the lake.
- Gadara: A Decapolis city above the Yarmuk valley.
- Gerasa: A large Decapolis city east of the Jordan.

## Key terms
- Tanakh: The Hebrew Bible: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets), Ketuvim (Writings). 'The Law and the Prophets' points to it.
- Remez: A 'hint': a short phrase that calls a whole Old Testament passage to mind. The captions spell it several ways.
- Halakha: From the Hebrew for 'walk': how one lives out the Torah day to day.
- Mitzvot: Commandments (singular mitzvah), and by extension the good deeds that obey them. The video calls them the fruit on the tree of halakha.
- Chiasm: A mirrored pattern; the video reads the sermon's ending as echoing its beginning.
- False prophets: Those who claim to speak for God but do not (Jeremiah 23:16). Jesus says they are known by their fruits.
- Lawlessness (anomia): Literally 'without law': the charge against those who never obeyed (7:23). [Background]
- Authority (exousia): The right and power to command. Jesus taught on His own authority (7:29). [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- City gates: The gate was where elders judged, business was done and news was shared. In Proverbs, Wisdom stands at the gates to call the city.
- Wolves and shepherds: Wolves were a real danger to flocks. Prophets used them for rulers who preyed on the people (Zephaniah 3:3; Ezekiel 22:27).
- Building in Galilee: Houses were built of basalt stones. In the rainy season, dry stream beds can flood suddenly; a house on bedrock stands, one on sand washes out.
- Teaching with authority: Scribes taught by citing earlier teachers. Jesus' 'But I say to you' in chapter 5 stunned the crowds (7:28-29).

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "But look not to this, says He, that it is rough and narrow, but where it ends; nor that the opposite is wide and spacious, but where it issues." Homilies on Matthew 23, on 7:13-14. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "He calls the steadfastness of His doctrine a rock; because in truth His commands are stronger than any rock, setting one above all the waves of human affairs." Homilies on Matthew 24, on 7:24-25. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Do 'abolish' and 'fulfill' mean 'misinterpret' and 'interpret'? The video holds this view, popular in some Jewish-roots teaching. Many scholars read 'fulfill' in Matthew as bringing to its intended goal, as with prophecy fulfilled (1:22; 2:15). Either way, 5:17-48 shows Jesus giving the true sense of the Law.
- Who are the false prophets? The video: the Jewish religious leaders of Jesus' day. Others see a warning for the church's future too, as in 24:11 and Acts 20:29-30.
- Is the sermon a chiasm? Several outlines propose a mirrored shape (for example the bookends 5:17 and 7:12). Not every scholar agrees on the details.
- Does 7:21-23 deny that the miracles happened? Jesus does not dispute their claims; He says He never knew them. Works done 'in Your name' are not the same as doing the Father's will.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- On screen the fruitful tree is Psalm 1:1-3 (the captions say 'Psalm 11 1:3'), and the evening wolves are Zephaniah 3:3 (the captions say 'Zephaniah 33').
- Mitzvot literally means 'commandments' (singular mitzvah). It is also used for good deeds, which is the video's point.
- In Jeremiah 23:11 the Hebrew is the verb chanaph (H2610), 'polluted' in the LSB. The 'hypocrite' sense belongs to the related word chaneph (H2611), 'godless' in the LSB (Job 8:13), which older English Bibles render 'hypocrite.'
- That 'abolish' and 'fulfill' are idioms for interpreting is the video's view; scholars debate it (see Debates).
- In the video's reading of 5:17, 'the Law of the Prophets' should be 'the Law or the Prophets.'

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. What makes the narrow gate hard to find, and the wide gate easy to walk through?
2. The video says the two gates can look alike. How would you tell Wisdom's call from Folly's today?
3. How would you check a teacher's fruit against the Beatitudes, without becoming the judge 7:1-5 warns about?
4. Is it possible to love your ministry for God more than God? What are the warning signs?
5. Which of Jesus' words in chapters 5-7 are you hearing but not yet doing?
6. Rewatch the video, as the teacher suggests. What did you notice the second time?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: it is possible for respected religious leaders who teach and observe God's word with authority to be far from the Lord and ignore what matters to Him. Disciples should watch not just what teachers say, however correct, but whether their fruit matches the sermon. For us: are there those who know and teach God's word but are far from the Lord in their hearts? You will know by watching what they do, and seeing if it aligns with the Beatitudes and Jesus' examples. Think about how this applies to your life so that you can do something about it.
- Study note (added): turn the test on yourself first (7:5). Pick one Beatitude this week and ask, 'Does my life bear this fruit?' Then do one concrete thing Jesus said in chapters 5-7, since the wise builder is the one who 'hears these words of Mine and does them' (7:24).
